# Scepticism towards astrology, omens, witchcraft and transmutation (`scepticism_superstition`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/ideas.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`)
- Deps: helped by natural_causes, selection_bias_sampling, controlled_trial
- Core idea: Divination, astrology, witchcraft accusations and gold-making share one weakness: their successes are remembered and their failures explained away, and when hits and misses are all written down beforehand and counted they do no better than chance. Old and respectable arguments are available: twins born under the same stars have different fates, and thousands with different horoscopes die in one battle (Cicero, Augustine); confessions of witchcraft obtained by torture prove only that pain makes people say anything (Spee); no alchemist has ever sold gold cheaper than the mint. The fair test is to have the practitioner state specific predictions in writing, seal them, and compare. Be precise about alchemy: its transmutation of lead into gold fails, but its furnaces, acids and distillation are real chemistry.
- Pitfalls:
  - Treating astrology as a fringe belief: in 1490 it is taught in medical faculties and practised at every court, and Tycho, Kepler and Galileo cast horoscopes
  - Calling the witch craze medieval; the great hunts fall about 1560–1650, and total executions are estimated at roughly 40,000–60,000, not millions
  - Denying the reality of witches where the Malleus Maleficarum (1486) calls that denial itself heresy; argue about proof and torture instead
  - Dismissing alchemists as frauds; they developed the laboratory methods chemistry inherited, and Boyle and Newton practised it
  - Ruining a court astrologer or diviner without offering the ruler something more useful makes a deadly, well-connected enemy
- History: mesopotamia: 2nd–1st millennium BC – omen series (Enuma Anu Enlil) are state science; horoscopes appear c. 410 BC; no known sceptical tradition; greece: 2nd c. BC – Carneades' arguments against astrology; c. 180 AD Lucian exposes the oracle-monger Alexander of Abonoteichus; rome: 44 BC – Cicero, De divinatione; c. 400 AD Augustine's twins argument; china: c. 250 BC – Xunzi: omens are rare natural events, to be wondered at but not feared; c. 80 AD Wang Chong, Lunheng, criticises claims that the dead harm the living, while accepting personal destiny; india: early Buddhist texts list divination among livelihoods monks should avoid; later sources preserve materialist criticisms of sacrificial rites attributed to the Carvakas; islamic: c. 1021 – Ibn Sina denies that alchemists can transmute species of metal; 1194 Maimonides' letter against astrology (written in Egypt); 1377 Ibn Khaldun refutes astrology and alchemy in the Muqaddimah; europe: c. 906 – Canon Episcopi calls night-flying a delusion; c. 1360s Oresme against divination; 1496 Pico della Mirandola's Disputations against astrology (Florence); 1563 Weyer; 1584 Scot; 1631 Spee, Cautio criminalis; global: 1985 – Carlson's double-blind test of astrologers in Nature finds chance-level results
- Read:
  - Cicero, De divinatione (44 BC)
  - Keith Thomas, Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971)
  - Carl Sagan, The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark (1995)
